doc.title: Lorraine Feather interviewed by Monk Rowe, via Zoom, March 22, 2023

title: 'I Love You Guys' and writing for an audience
summary: The piano doubling her melody, Shelly's drummer jokes, a nod to husband Tony Morales, and timing laughs.

story.theme_name: Teaching jazz: schools, students and advice to the young
story.community_name: Playing for the audience: communicating from the bandstand

blocks.x: There was an interesting moment in your tune, “I Love You Guys” where I think it was just the first two lines that you sang. The piano was playing the melody with you and I wondered, I don’t know if it was planned or was it spontaneous but it was a nice effect and you don’t usually hear it because singers don’t usually want that. Do you recall that? © Fillius Jazz Archive -8-

Yes. I had forgotten, but you’re right. It is a nice effect that we use sometimes. And I might sing in unison with Charlie Bisharat, the violinist, or with the pianist, in that case it was Shelly. He — I know that at the beginning of that tune he wanted it to be about journeymen musicians who are doing all these gigs and a lot of them were horrible. And he wanted to sound like he was kind of in a lounge overplaying. But we had a lot of fun. I really like it. Oh and then there’s a line in “I Love You Guys”, “I love it when you take it ‘round the bend together then you suddenly and mysteriously end together — and Shelly said it should just be complete chaos and then all of a sudden you suddenly mysteriously end together. And everybody got a kick out of that because it’s part of their lives. So you know, and I also put a thing in there about a seven-stroke roll — your license plate — I’ve dated a ton of you, married one of you, his license plate was a seven-stroke roll. That was just a little nod to my husband of almost 30 years, Tony Morales. Although I believe my ex-brother-in-law is the one who has the seven-stroke roll on his license plate. But it’s an inside drummer thing that most people wouldn’t know but I like to make the guys laugh.

That’s an interesting thing to think about inside. Have you ever listened — had your music playing with a small group of people and you’re there and some of these lyric things you do come up. Do you watch these people to see if they’re sort of chuckling at the parts that you hope they chuckle to?

Oh yeah. Yeah. I haven’t been performing in some time because I’ve been more focused on writing lyrics and doing my own projects, but yes, I notice that in the audience. And you have to think about whether or not you want to put a little interlude after something that you consider funny, just so that the beginning of the next line doesn’t get drowned in laughter.
